newsitem.title: USA: Monsanto-Pioneer biotech suits add to legal tangle.
newsitem.headline: Monsanto-Pioneer biotech suits add to legal tangle.

text.p: A lawsuit and countersuit filed by Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc and Monsanto Co over patent rights add to the legal tangle involving agricultural biotechnology, with no immediate settlements expected.
"Nothing is going to be resolved this year, and we've got more legal confusion ahead," said Natwest Securities analyst Mark Wiltamuth.
Monsanto said Friday it filed a counterclaim to a contract lawsuit that was brought against it in late March by Pioneer.
Both Pioneer's suit and Monsanto's counterclaim revolve around genetics to make biotech corn that is resistant to the European corn borer, a major crop pest.
These suits are the latest in a series of legal actions taken by the major players in agricultural biotechnology.

At the same time, companies have been developing technologies and forging alliances to build a portfolio of genes to enhance crops -- such as making them resistant to certain insect pests or able to withstand use of a herbicide to kill weeds in the field.

"The industry as a whole needs to work through those (patent) rights...," Pioneer spokesman Tim Martin said. "Whether or not it's going to be the industry members who negotiate settlements or if it takes court actions, it's hard to say."

The latest legal action involves Monsanto's countersuit which, among other things, seeks to terminate a 1993 agreement under which Pioneer licensed Monsanto's Bt gene for corn. Monsanto also is seeking a $10 million milestone payment from Pioneer as part of the research agreement.
Martin said Pioneer put the payment due Monsanto in an escrow account until the dispute is resolved.

Pioneer, which holds about 44 percent of the North American seed corn market, has sued Monsanto to secure rights to patents held by DeKalb Genetics Corp. Monsanto has a large, minority stake in DeKalb.
"They should be able to give us rights and cross-licensing with the technology that DeKalb has," Martin said. "That was part of the agreement."
Monsanto has countered that it is only an investor in DeKalb and does not control that seed company's technology.
Natwest's Wiltamuth said that, despite the lawsuits, he does not expect Pioneer and Monsanto, an agricultural, pharmaceutical and food ingredients company, to sever ties.
"The two companies need each other," he said, citing Monsanto's biotech gene portfolio and Pioneer's leading presence in the North American seed corn market.
"I'm sure that at some point a settlement will come out of it," he added.
Beyond the 1993 license agreement, Pioneer and Monsanto in the past pursued a potential merger, Pioneer's Martin acknowledged.

"A few years ago Monsanto had approached Pioneer about the possibility of a merger or acquisition," Martin said. "We were approached and talks happened. But Pioneer has always been interested in maintaining our independence."
